Summarize the following technical article in 5 bullet points, then list any claims you think need a citation.

Consistent Hashing and Semantic Caching in LLM Gateways: A Technical Overview

Introduction

Modern applications built on large language models face a recurring economic problem: every call to a hosted model costs money and time, and a large fraction of real-world traffic consists of requests that are semantically identical or near-identical to requests already served moments earlier. A user asking "what's the capital of France" and a second user asking "can you tell me the capital city of France" are, from the model's point of view, asking for the same answer. Serving the second request from a cache rather than paying for a second inference call is one of the highest-leverage optimizations available to an LLM gateway operator, provided the cache can be made both fast and safe.

This document surveys the two technical building blocks that make this possible at scale: consistent hashing, which is the general distributed-systems technique for routing keys to cache nodes without wholesale reshuffling when nodes are added or removed, and semantic caching, which is the LLM-specific technique for deciding whether two different pieces of text mean the same thing closely enough to reuse a cached answer.

Part One: Consistent Hashing

In a traditional cache cluster, a naive approach to deciding which node holds a given key is to compute hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes. This works fine until N changes. The moment a node is added or removed, almost every key's assigned node changes, because the modulus changes. In a cache serving millions of keys, this means a single node failure or a single scaling event invalidates nearly the entire cache, causing a stampede of cache misses against the origin (in this case, the upstream LLM provider) at exactly the moment the system is already under stress from a topology change.

Consistent hashing solves this by mapping both nodes and keys onto the same abstract space, typically visualized as a ring of hash values from 0 to some large maximum (2^32 - 1 is common). Each node is assigned one or more positions on this ring, usually by hashing the node's identifier (such as its hostname or IP address) with several different hash functions or salts, producing multiple points per physical node. These are called virtual nodes, and they exist specifically to smooth out the distribution of keys across physical nodes, since a small number of hash points per node can otherwise lead to significant load imbalance.

A key is assigned to whichever node's position is the first one encountered walking clockwise around the ring from the key's own hash position. When a node is added, it only needs to take ownership of the keys that fall between its new position and the position of the previous node going counter-clockwise; it does not affect the assignment of any other key on the ring. Conversely, when a node is removed, only the keys it owned need to be reassigned, to the next node clockwise. In both cases, the fraction of keys that move is roughly 1/N, not nearly 100% as in the modulus approach. This property, that adding or removing a node only disturbs a small, bounded fraction of the total keyspace, is the entire reason consistent hashing exists and is used pervasively in systems such as Amazon's Dynamo, Cassandra, and many CDN edge caching layers.

For an LLM gateway backed by a Redis cluster or a sharded Postgres/pgvector deployment, consistent hashing (or an equivalent partitioning scheme, since some systems such as Redis Cluster use hash slots instead, which achieve a similar goal via a different mechanism) matters for the same reason: as the cache tier scales horizontally to handle growing query volume, the operator wants scaling events to cause a small, predictable amount of cache churn, not a catastrophic mass eviction that dumps the full request volume back onto the origin LLM providers at the worst possible moment.

Part Two: Semantic Caching

Traditional caching keys on exact string equality: the same request produces the same cache key, and only byte-identical requests hit. This is useless for LLM gateways in practice, because natural language has enormous surface variation for the same underlying intent. "What's the capital of France?" and "Can you tell me the capital city of France?" are different strings but the same question. A naive exact-match cache would treat these as entirely unrelated and issue two full-price calls to the upstream model.

Semantic caching instead embeds each incoming prompt into a fixed-length vector representation using a sentence embedding model (a common lightweight choice is a distilled sentence-transformer such as MiniLM-L6, producing 384-dimensional vectors, chosen for its balance of embedding quality against latency and index size compared to larger embedding models). When a new request arrives, its embedding is computed and compared against the embeddings of recently cached requests using a similarity metric, typically cosine similarity. If the closest existing cache entry's similarity exceeds a chosen threshold, the cached response is returned instead of calling the upstream model.

The central engineering challenge in semantic caching is choosing that threshold. Set it too low, and semantically different prompts get treated as equivalent, a false hit, which is far worse than a cache miss because it silently returns a wrong answer to the user rather than merely costing a bit more money and latency. Set it too high, and legitimate paraphrases fail to hit, and the cache captures little of the available savings. This tradeoff is best visualized as a precision-recall curve: sweeping the similarity threshold from a low value to a high value (a typical sweep range is 0.80 to 0.99 in increments of 0.01) and, for each threshold, measuring the hit rate against a labelled corpus of true paraphrases and the false-hit rate against a labelled corpus of adversarial near-misses, produces a curve from which an operator can pick a defensible operating point rather than guessing.

Adversarial near-misses deserve special attention because embedding-based similarity is fundamentally a bag-of-meaning comparison; it is not naturally sensitive to the kind of single-token changes that completely flip the correct answer to a question. "Is aspirin safe to take during pregnancy?" and "Is aspirin not safe to take during pregnancy?" differ by a single word, but cosine similarity between their embeddings is typically extremely high, often above 0.95, because the overall semantic content, the topic, the entities, and most of the surface form, is nearly identical. A naive threshold set to catch ordinary paraphrases will very likely also catch this negation, silently serving the wrong cached answer to a safety-relevant medical question.

This is the motivation for an entity guard, a secondary check layered on top of the embedding similarity score. Before serving a cache hit, the guard extracts salient entities from both the incoming prompt and the candidate cached prompt, numbers, dates, named entities, and negation markers, and if these disagree, the hit is rejected regardless of how high the cosine similarity score was, and the request falls through to the upstream model. Measuring the effect of the entity guard is itself an experiment worth publishing: running the same threshold sweep with the guard enabled and disabled and quantifying exactly how much false-hit rate the guard removes, and how much legitimate recall it costs (since an overly aggressive guard can also reject some true paraphrases that happen to contain differing but semantically compatible entities), turns a design decision into a measured, defensible number rather than an assumption.

Part Three: Interaction Between the Two Layers

In a fully realized gateway architecture, these two techniques operate at different layers and largely do not interfere with each other, but they do compose. The semantic cache's vector index, whether implemented with pgvector's HNSW index or a dedicated vector database, still needs to be distributed as query volume and corpus size grow, and the same consistent-hashing-style partitioning principles that apply to a plain key-value cache apply to sharding a vector index as well, albeit with the added complexity that a similarity search may in principle need to check candidates across shard boundaries, unlike an exact-key lookup which is always routed deterministically to exactly one shard.

The practical takeaway for anyone designing this kind of system is that the two problems, "where do I store this data so scaling doesn't wreck the cache," and "how do I decide whether two different pieces of text mean the same thing," are genuinely separate concerns that are easy to conflate when first learning about caching, and treating them as such, with independent, measurable design decisions for each, is what separates a system that merely works from one whose behavior can be explained, tuned, and trusted under load.

Summary

Consistent hashing bounds the blast radius of scaling events on a distributed cache to roughly 1/N of the keyspace, rather than the near-total invalidation caused by naive modulus hashing. Semantic caching converts natural-language surface variation into a similarity search problem, using sentence embeddings and a tuned cosine similarity threshold, with an entity guard as a necessary safeguard against high-similarity, low-integrity adversarial near-misses such as single-word negations or single-digit numeric changes. Both techniques are measurable, tunable, and worth publishing real numbers about rather than treating as fixed defaults.

prompt:
Read the following meeting transcript and extract: (1) all decisions made, (2) all action items with owners, (3) any open questions left unresolved.

Meeting Transcript: Aether Gateway - M4 Semantic Cache Design Review
Date: internal planning session
Attendees: Priya (backend lead), Marcus (SRE), Wei (data/ML), Sam (product)

Priya: Okay, let's get started. Today's agenda is the semantic cache design for M4. We need to land on the embedding model, the similarity threshold, the entity guard approach, and the invalidation strategy before anyone starts writing code. Wei, you've been running the offline experiments, want to kick us off?

Wei: Sure. So I benchmarked three embedding models against the labelled corpus: MiniLM-L6, which is 384 dimensions and pretty small, a larger BGE-base model at 768 dimensions, and OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small as a cloud baseline for comparison even though we're not using it in production. On the near-duplicate bucket, MiniLM gets about 89% recall at a 0.94 threshold, BGE gets about 93%, and the cloud model gets about 95%. But latency is where it gets interesting. MiniLM embeds a typical prompt in about 8 milliseconds on CPU. BGE takes about 22 milliseconds. And obviously the cloud model has network latency on top, call it 150 to 300 milliseconds depending on region.

Marcus: What about index size? If we're running this on the free tier Oracle box we don't have infinite RAM.

Wei: Right, so for 500k cached entries, MiniLM's 384-dim vectors work out to about 768KB per thousand entries at float32, so roughly 384MB for the full 500k. BGE at 768 dimensions roughly doubles that to about 768MB. Given we're targeting a 24GB box total, shared with Postgres, Redis, the gateway JVM itself, Prometheus, Grafana, and Ollama, that's a meaningful chunk of headroom either way, but BGE eats a lot more of it for a few points of recall.

Priya: So what's the recommendation?

Wei: I'd go with MiniLM for the baseline system, and write up the comparison as one of the benchmark experiments, since PRD section 16.2 explicitly asks for an embedding model comparison with accuracy, latency, and index size tradeoffs reported. The story isn't "MiniLM is best," it's "MiniLM is the right tradeoff for this deployment target, and here's the number that proves it."

Sam: That's a good story for the writeup. Let's go with that. What about the threshold?

Wei: Threshold sweep results are attached in the doc I shared, but the short version: at 0.90 we get high recall, around 92%, but false-hit rate on the adversarial bucket climbs to almost 15%, which is way too high given some of those adversarial examples are things like drug interaction warnings. At 0.97 false-hit rate drops under 1%, but recall drops to about 71%, so we're leaving a lot of savings on the table. 0.94 looks like the sweet spot in the curve, roughly 85% recall with about 3% false-hit rate before the entity guard even kicks in.

Marcus: And after the guard?

Wei: With the guard on, false-hit rate at 0.94 drops from about 3% to under 0.5%, and recall only drops a couple points, to about 82%, because the guard is pretty targeted, it only rejects hits where the extracted numbers or negation markers actually disagree. So the guard is doing real work for cheap.

Priya: Okay, 0.94 with the guard on, that matches the number in the PRD's example sentence almost exactly, that's not a coincidence, that's roughly what a system like this tends to land on. Let's lock that as the default and make it configurable per model since some models might warrant a different threshold later.

Sam: What about invalidation? If a cached answer turns out to be stale, how do we clear it?

Priya: Three mechanisms. TTL-based expiry, we're defaulting to six hours for now, that's configurable per cache entry. Manual invalidation by entry ID, for when an operator finds a specific bad cache hit. And bulk invalidation by model ID, for when we roll a provider or model version and want to flush everything cached against the old one, since a new model version might answer differently even to the exact same prompt.

Marcus: Are we going to log every cache decision? I want to be able to debug false hits after the fact without guessing.

Wei: Yes, every lookup, hit or miss, gets logged with the similarity score, whether the guard was triggered, and the entry ID if it hit. That feeds directly into the request log for M5 observability, so this isn't extra work, it's just making sure the semantic cache module writes into the same structured log the rest of the system already uses.

Priya: Good. Sam, anything from the product side before we wrap?

Sam: Just a reminder that AC3 and AC4 are the numbers that matter externally, hit rate above 35% and a defensible false-hit rate. Whatever threshold we land on needs the corpus behind it to actually prove those numbers, not just look reasonable in a design doc. Wei, how's corpus labelling going?

Wei: About a quarter done across most buckets as of this week. Long-context is behind the others, that bucket takes real documents, not quick paraphrases, so it's slower going, but the rest are in decent shape for the threshold sweep to be meaningful once M4 starts.

Priya: Alright. Let's write this up: MiniLM-L6 for embeddings, 0.94 cosine threshold, entity guard on numbers and negation, six-hour TTL default plus manual and bulk invalidation, and every lookup logged with its similarity score. Action items: Wei, finish the threshold sweep writeup with the actual charts by end of week. Marcus, spec out the pgvector HNSW index parameters, we still need to pick m and ef_search before this ships. Sam, update the milestone doc with the locked decisions. I'll open the ADR. Anything else? Okay, thanks everyone.

prompt:
Read the following API reference document and list every distinct HTTP status code it defines, along with the condition that triggers it.

Aether Gateway API Reference (Draft)

Overview

This document describes the HTTP API surface exposed by the Aether Gateway. The gateway sits between client applications and one or more upstream LLM providers, adding routing, resilience, quota enforcement, semantic caching, and observability without requiring clients to speak provider-specific protocols. All endpoints are versioned under a common prefix and return structured JSON error bodies on failure, following RFC 9457 problem-details conventions.

Authentication

Every request must include an API key in the Authorization header, formatted as a bearer token: Authorization: Bearer <key>. Keys are issued per tenant and are associated with a monthly budget and a set of allowed models. A request with a missing or invalid key returns 401 Unauthorized with a problem-details body indicating the reason. A request from a valid key that has exceeded its monthly budget returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header set to the number of seconds until the next budget reset, and a body indicating current spend versus the configured limit.

Endpoint: POST /v1/chat/completions

This is the primary endpoint and mirrors the OpenAI chat completions shape closely enough that most existing client SDKs can point at the gateway with only a base URL change. The request body accepts a model field, a messages array of role/content pairs, and standard sampling parameters such as temperature, top_p, and max_tokens. Two gateway-specific fields are supported in addition to the standard shape: routing_policy, which can be set to cost_optimized, latency_optimized, or a specific provider name to bypass automatic routing, and cache_bypass, a boolean that, when true, skips the semantic cache lookup entirely and always calls the upstream model, useful for clients that need a guaranteed fresh response regardless of cache state.

When stream is set to true in the request body, the response is returned as a Server-Sent Events stream, with each event carrying a JSON-encoded delta chunk in the same shape as the non-streaming response's choices array, terminated by a final event with data: [DONE]. The gateway proxies the upstream provider's stream chunk-by-chunk rather than buffering the full response, which keeps time-to-first-token low. If the client disconnects mid-stream, the gateway propagates the cancellation to the upstream provider's connection rather than letting it run to completion and discarding the result, since that would waste both money and provider quota on a response nobody will read.

Response headers on every completions call, streaming or not, include X-Aether-Cache-Status, one of hit, miss, or bypassed, and X-Aether-Provider, indicating which upstream provider actually served the request. X-Aether-Cost-USD reports the estimated cost of the call based on the provider's published per-token pricing, which is what the cost simulation experiments in the benchmark suite are built from.

Endpoint: GET /v1/models

Returns the list of models currently available through the gateway, aggregated across all configured providers, along with the routing policy default for each and whether each provider adapter currently reports itself healthy. A model with an unhealthy provider is still listed, but is annotated with a status field of degraded, so clients can proactively avoid routing new requests to it rather than discovering the failure on the next completion call.

Endpoint: GET /v1/usage

Returns the calling tenant's current-period usage: total requests, total tokens (prompt and completion separately), estimated spend, budget limit, and cache hit rate over the period. This endpoint is what a billing dashboard or an internal cost-tracking tool would poll. It is intentionally cheap to call, backed by pre-aggregated counters rather than a live scan of the request log, so it is safe to poll frequently without adding load to the request-logging path.

Endpoint: POST /v1/admin/cache/invalidate

Restricted to keys with an admin scope. Accepts either an entry_id to invalidate a single cached response, or a model_id to bulk-invalidate every cached entry associated with that model, used when a provider ships a new model version and previously cached responses may no longer reflect how the model would answer today. Returns a count of entries invalidated.

Endpoint: GET /v1/admin/breaker-status

Restricted to admin scope. Returns the current circuit breaker state, closed, open, or half_open, for each configured provider, along with the failure count in the current rolling window and the timestamp of the last state transition. This exists specifically so an operator debugging a degraded experience can immediately tell whether requests are being routed away from a provider due to an open breaker, rather than having to infer it from latency graphs alone.

Error semantics

All error responses follow the same structure: a type URI identifying the error category, a human-readable title, a status field matching the HTTP status code, and a detail field with request-specific context. Common status codes: 400 for malformed request bodies, such as a messages array with no entries or an unsupported role value. 401 for missing or invalid authentication. 403 for a valid key attempting to use a model it is not authorized for. 404 for a reference to a model_id or entry_id that does not exist, used on the admin invalidation endpoint. 429 for budget or rate limit exhaustion, always accompanied by a Retry-After header. 502 when every configured provider for a requested model is currently unavailable, meaning the circuit breaker is open on all of them and there is no healthy fallback to route to. 504 when the gateway's own timeout for a non-streaming request is exceeded waiting on an upstream provider, distinct from a provider-reported error, since it indicates the gateway itself gave up rather than the provider explicitly failing.

Rate limiting

Rate limits are enforced per tenant using a token bucket algorithm backed by Redis, so limits are consistent across all gateway instances in a horizontally scaled deployment rather than being tracked per-instance. Each tenant's bucket capacity and refill rate are configured as part of their plan. When a request is rejected due to rate limiting rather than budget exhaustion, the response still uses 429 but the problem-details type field distinguishes rate-limit-exceeded from budget-exceeded, since clients typically want to handle these differently: a rate limit suggests backing off and retrying shortly, while a budget limit suggests the request will keep failing until the next billing period regardless of retry timing.

Idempotency

Chat completion requests are not idempotent by default, since resubmitting the same messages array with cache_bypass true will genuinely produce two separate billed calls to the upstream provider, by design. Clients that need idempotency for retry-safety should supply an Idempotency-Key header; the gateway will return the cached response for a previous request with the same key within a 24-hour window rather than re-executing it, distinct from the semantic cache, since this is exact-match idempotency keyed on the client-supplied header value, not similarity-based.

Versioning

The v1 prefix is stable; breaking changes will be introduced under a new prefix rather than modifying v1's existing behavior. Additive changes, such as new optional fields, new response headers, or new endpoints, may be introduced under v1 without a version bump, following standard API evolution practice for maintaining backward compatibility.
